text: 1.2 Hello and thank you all for coming. I know you're all busy students and I appreciate that you're here today. As we all know, there are many animals which are disappearing from our planet. Rhinos, orangutans, sea turtles, the list is shocking. Now, what do you think of when you hear African elephant? Perhaps something like intelligent, majestic, powerful. Now, even though these words describe these creatures perfectly, those three qualities may not be enough to save them. A century ago, there were around 5 million elephants across Africa. Today, it is believed that there are less than 500,000. In fact, both species of African elephants are endangered. While people are generally more familiar with the Savannah elephant, I'm here today to talk about the African forest elephant, which is smaller, less well known, and it's critically endangered because of the threat that it faces from humans. The main human threat to forest elephants comes from poachers, who hunt them for their long, white, beautiful tusks. It's widely known that these tusks are made of ivory, a material that poachers sell to make a lot of money, even though it's illegal. The international trade of ivory was banned in 1989, yet several countries still allow ivory to be bought and sold across their borders. This has actually increased over recent years. The second threat is the loss of the elephant's habitat, which happens when humans destroy rainforest areas to make the land suitable for farming. This means the elephants have less space to live in, so the food they depend on for survival, such as fruit, grasses, and leaves, not only becomes less available, but also has to be shared between the same number of elephants. A third threat is contact between humans and elephants. Habitat loss sometimes forces elephants to leave the rainforest and go into villages, where they damage crops growing in farmers' fields. Because of this, local people sometimes kill the elephants. They see this as the only way to protect themselves, their families, their food, and their homes. However, there is good news. It may not be too late to save the African forest elephant, but there are several things that really ought to happen first. First, there needs to be an increase in the number of specially trained guards who work in the rainforests to catch the poachers. Second, governments must introduce an immediate and complete ban on anyone buying or selling ivory, even between countries sharing a border. Third, we have to find ways of reducing contact between humans and elephants. For instance, local communities should be helped to build suitable fences that can protect their land. So, to summarize, as well as habitat loss and human contact, the main threat to forest elephants comes from poaching. We've got to end the illegal trade of ivory. The governments and environmental organizations who can do this must not delay for a moment longer. Without a ban, the African forest elephant may soon become extinct.
